title: Songs of mourning
hook: Guru Nanak's dirges are sung for the dead, remembering that all must go (Vadhans M1, ang 578)

segments.voice: Yesterday, be a renunciant at home, and your line: the forest at home. Did you find a minute of stillness in a busy room? This part of the path has sung for weddings and births. Today it sings at the other turning point. Day six hundred seventy-four.

In old Punjab, when someone died, the women of the village gathered in the courtyard. They sat in a circle and wailed, a lament with a rhythm to it, one woman leading, the others answering, beating their chests. The custom was called siapa, and the lament songs were alaahnees. Some families even hired professional mourners to lead them. Grief was loud, public, and shaped by tradition. Guru Nanak knew those songs. And he did something unexpected with them: he wrote his own. Today: songs of mourning.
screen: `WOMEN GATHERED IN A COURTYARD.` → `A LAMENT WITH A RHYTHM.` → `GURU NANAK WROTE HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, his laments, are in Raag Vadhans, starting on Ang five seventy-eight. He kept the form people knew, but changed what it sang about. The first one begins, in paraphrase: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. When the measure of a life is full, the soul is taken, and loved ones cry out. The body and soul are parted when the days are done. Notice the first word. A mourning song that opens with blessed. It doesn't deny the grief; the hymn says plainly that the family weeps. But it sets the grief inside something larger: a Creator who gives each life its span. Then the refrain-like truth that runs through these songs: everyone who comes must go. The king and the beggar, the young and the old. It's not said to scold anyone for crying. It's said the way a friend at a funeral says, gently, this is the road we all walk. Sikh practice took this to heart. At a Sikh funeral, the family doesn't hire mourners or beat their chests. Kirtan is sung, often Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas is said. Many families hold a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib in the days after. The alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung. Grief is allowed. But it's held in praise, and in the plain, shared knowledge that this is how every life goes.
screen: `ALAAHNEES: THE OLD LAMENTS.` · `A DIRGE THAT OPENS WITH BLESSED.` · `EVERYONE WHO COMES MUST GO.` · `GRIEF HELD IN PRAISE.` · then, large: `ALL MUST GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone gently. Sit, and bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet. Don't reach for the hardest memory. Let an ordinary one come: their laugh, a meal, a phrase they used. Let any sadness be there too. Then, quietly, give thanks that they were given the days they had. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Alaahnee. A lament, the old Punjabi mourning song. Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa keep its form but open with praise, and remember that everyone who comes must go.
Your line: all must go. Today, tell someone you love one thing you're glad about in them, while you're both here. Day six hundred seventy-four.

screen: `DAY 674 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DEATH OF THE BRAVE.`

howItsDone: At Sikh funerals and in the days after, families gather for kirtan, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, and Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung, in place of the old custom of ritual wailing.
